title: The birth, in verse
hookLine: the queen's dream, the grove, the child who takes seven steps (Buddhacarita 1)

lines: A DREAM OF A WHITE ELEPHANT.
cards: A queen lies asleep, and in her dream a white elephant enters her side. In time she asks to go out to a grove called Lumbini. The king agrees, she goes with her women, and there, in the grove, the child is born.
Year one told these scenes quickly, almost like a list. The poet won't hurry. He stops at the moment of birth and reaches for the old stories of India to compare it with.
And then he lets the newborn do something no newborn does.

teach.h: A BIRTH AMONG THE GREAT BIRTHS.
teach.b: First, the comparison. The child comes from his mother's side, and the poet lines this up with the births of heroes and kings in older Indian legend: one born from a thigh, one from a hand, one from the head.
The point isn't anatomy. It's company: this birth belongs with the great births his listeners already knew. Second, the steps.
As soon as he is born, the poem says, the child stands and takes seven steps, firm and steady. Then he speaks.
In paraphrase, he says he is born for awakening and for the good of the world, and that this birth is his last. Third, the world answers.

teach.h: WATER FROM THE SKY, COOL AND WARM.
teach.b: Streams of water fall from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him, and flowers come down on the grove. And fourth, the mother. It was Maya's wish that took everyone to Lumbini.
Year two told that she died soon after the birth, and the poem will say so too, in the next canto. So these first steps are taken in a grove his mother chose, by a child she won't see grow.
Seven steps is where the poem puts the start of the road.
The leaving, the searching, the sitting: every later scene is more steps on it.

how: Some Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth at festivals such as Vesak, and in some East Asian temples images of the newborn standing with one hand raised are bathed with sweet tea or water to recall the streams from the sky.

practice: Stand if you can, or let your hand do the walking on your knee, and take seven slow steps, counting each one: lift, feel it move, set it down. At seven, stop and feel your weight on the ground.
Then sit, and let the seven steps settle.
